answers.answer_2026: any conviction (even minor administrative offenses) can lead to loss of residence status
answers.change_2023_2026: There have been no right protections neither in 2023 nor in 2026
answers.implementation_then_now: The protection answer is the lowest option, so implementation is Does Not Apply on both dates. For context: HRW (World Report 2023) reports the Migration Service continued deporting people with criminal records. The OECD International Migration Outlook 2025 reports 1,100 expulsions in 2024 (690 administrative, 410 judicial for crimes), the most administrative expulsions in seven years.

practice_sources.title: Human Rights Watch, World Report 2023 - Chile

answers.sourcing_note: I read the LeyChile version table for Ley 21.325 (amendments by Leyes 21.590, 21.589, 21.610, 21.655, 21.730, 21.816) and each amending act. None touched Arts. 32, 33 or 88-90 before 1 Jan 2026. The 2023 text is rebuilt from the current consolidated text plus those acts, because the versioned text would not load.
answers.starting_answer_concern: Partly debatable. Art. 89 (through Art. 32 Nos. 5-6) and Art. 90 (through Art. 33) tie revocation to crimes and misdemeanours (crimen o simple delito). Administrative sanctions count only indirectly: Art. 90 No. 4 (unpaid fines for serious migration infractions) and Art. 88 No. 5 (repeated tax or social-security sanctions). A coder could also defend 'only major convictions'. Since 2 June 2026, Ley 21.816 Art. 3 added Art. 88 No. 6: rejection for being on the fare-evasion register, a minor administrative sanction. That supports the starting answer for November 2026.
answers.notes: Ley 21.816 (published and in force 2026-06-02) added Art. 88 No. 6 to Ley 21.325: 'Se encuentren en el Registro de Pasajeros Infractores de la ley N 18.287'. It is outside the window and is not recorded as an event. Ley 21.730 (in force 2025-04-01, creates the Ministerio de Seguridad Publica) is institutional only.

answers.change_2023_2026: There have been no right protections neither in 2023 nor in 2026

events.article: Ley 20.430 new Art. 28 bis; Ley 21.325 Art. 131 inciso 2
events.what_changed: Added an initial admissibility stage for refugee claims. Non-refoulement under Art. 4 applies during that stage. Border return (reconduccion) was widened to people found up to 10 km inside the border. The torture/CIDT clause of Art. 4 is untouched and still covers only asylum seekers and refugees, so the answer stays No.
events.passage: Durante esta etapa inicial se dara cumplimiento al principio de no devolucion, de conformidad con lo dispuesto en el articulo 4.

answers.implementation_then_now: Does Not Apply on both dates, because the answer is No. Border returns (reconducciones) without a protection assessment continued: CIPER reports 5,053 in 2025, mainly at Colchane.
answers.sourcing_note: The Ley 20.430 version table shows only the 2022 and 2024 (Ley 21.655) versions. The current Art. 4 carries no amendment note. I read Ley 21.655 in full.
answers.starting_answer_concern: Ley 20.430 Art. 4 inciso 2 expressly extends non-refoulement to cases where there are substantial grounds to believe the person would face torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. It covers asylum seekers as well as recognized refugees. q51 is coded Yes on the same article, and the Peru and Colombia examples were coded Yes on refugee-law provisions, so this No looks inconsistent.
answers.notes: No ruling in the window states a general rule extending the protection to all migrants.

answers.change_2023_2026: There have been right protections both in 2023 and 2026 but they are not the same

events.what_changed: Recognition under Art. 2 Nos. 1 and 2 now requires direct arrival (no more than 60 days in a third country). Ley 21.655 also added a 7-day filing deadline, an inadmissibility stage for manifestly unfounded claims (non-refoulement applies during it), and wider border returns under Art. 131 of Ley 21.325. The Art. 4 ban is unchanged.
events.passage: Solo tendran derecho a que se les reconozca la calidad de refugiado de conformidad con los numerales 1 y 2 quienes lleguen directamente desde el territorio en que su vida o libertad este amenazada.

answers.implementation_then_now: 2023: in Rol 115.005-2022 (March 2023) the Supreme Court found the Migration Service systematically refused to receive refugee claims from people who entered irregularly, and ordered a protocol. HRW reports 701 of about 22,000 claims granted between 2010 and 2021. 2026: the OECD reports 6% positive decisions in 2024, and CIPER reports 5,053 border returns in 2025. Neither source shows expulsions of people already in the procedure. Access barriers persist and stricter admissibility rules apply from 2024. No clear shift in practice.

answers.sourcing_note: The amendment is dated from the LeyChile annotation 'Ley 21655 Art. 1 N 1 D.O. 20.02.2024' and from the act itself. The practice evidence is indirect: I found no 2024-2025 report directly documenting returns of asylum seekers to persecution. PDFs (UPR, CMW, UDP) could not be read.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The starting rating 'Usually; Rarely' pairs non-neighbouring levels: likely Usually for people inside the procedure and Rarely at the border. The schema cannot express it, so Sometimes is entered as the closest single value.
answers.notes: The Supreme Court ruling was read only through a Poder Judicial press note, so it is used as practice evidence only.

answers.change_2023_2026: There have been no right protections neither in 2023 nor in 2026

events.what_changed: Recognition on the broadened ground (Art. 2 No. 2: generalized violence, massive human-rights violations) now requires direct arrival. The protection remains limited to asylum seekers and refugees, so the answer stays No.
events.passage: Solo tendran derecho a que se les reconozca la calidad de refugiado de conformidad con los numerales 1 y 2 quienes lleguen directamente desde el territorio en que su vida o libertad este amenazada.

answers.implementation_then_now: Does Not Apply on both dates, because the answer is No. Border returns without protection screening continued (CIPER: 5,053 in 2025).
answers.sourcing_note: The version table of Ley 20.430 and Ley 21.655 were both read. Art. 4 is unchanged.
answers.starting_answer_concern: Ley 20.430 Art. 4 bars return where 'estuviere en peligro la seguridad de la persona' and has authorities weigh mass human-rights violations. Ley 21.325 Art. 10 bars returning holders of complementary protection to a risk to life or integrity. Both cover only protection-seekers, but the MRD coded Peru Yes on comparable refugee-law provisions, so this No looks inconsistent.
